title: Repository pattern versus direct DbContext (when each helps)
hook: Wrapping DbContext in IRepository<Order> does not magically improve testability — EF Core DbContext is already mockable. The real question is whether the abstraction earns its keep or just adds indirection.

blocks.text: The repository pattern hides data access behind an interface like IOrderRepository with methods GetByIdAsync, ListAsync, AddAsync. Direct DbContext usage injects AppDbContext into handlers or application services and writes LINQ inline. EF Core's DbContext already implements repository and unit-of-work patterns — Microsoft guidance for most apps: use DbContext directly unless you have a specific reason for abstraction. Generic IRepository<T> with GetAll() often becomes a leaky CRUD wrapper that fights LINQ expressiveness. Useful abstractions: query objects, specification pattern, or domain-specific repositories with meaningful methods.

entries.plainDefinition: Abstraction over data access that exposes collection-like or domain-specific query methods.
entries.example: public interface IOrderRepository { Task<Order?> GetByIdAsync(Guid id); }

entries.plainDefinition: Single transaction boundary coordinating multiple repository writes — DbContext is the unit of work.
entries.example: SaveChangesAsync commits all pending changes in one transaction.

entries.plainDefinition: IRepository<T> with CRUD — often criticized as redundant over DbSet<T>.
Encapsulates query logic in reusable, composable objects.

blocks.text: This is a culture-war topic on r/dotnet and a common LeetCode system design follow-up. Interviewers test whether you parrot patterns blindly or choose based on testability, team boundaries, and query complexity. Wrong answer: 'always use repository for clean architecture.' Right answer: 'DbContext is the unit of work; I add abstraction when query logic repeats, when swapping data stores, or when domain language needs hiding — not a generic CRUD wrapper.'

blocks.title: Testing without repository
blocks.body: Use InMemory provider, SQLite in-memory, or Testcontainers with WebApplicationFactory — test against real EF behavior. Mocking DbContext is painful and tests nothing about SQL translation.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Start with DbContext
items.body: Default for ASP.NET Core APIs — inject AppDbContext, LINQ in application services.

items.title: Extract when logic repeats
items.body: Same complex query in 5 handlers → private method, specification, or domain repository.

items.title: Avoid generic IRepository<T>
items.body: GetAll() returning IQueryable leaks EF; CRUD methods duplicate DbSet.

items.title: Test with real provider
items.body: Integration tests over SQLite/Testcontainers — not mock repository.

diagram.title: Layering options
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  H[Minimal API / Controller] --> S[Application Service]
  S --> DC[AppDbContext direct\nrecommended default]
  S --> R[Domain Repository\nwhen query logic is complex]
  R --> DC
  S -.-> BAD[Generic IRepository T\nCRUD wrapper\navoid unless justified]

snippet.label: Direct DbContext — recommended default
snippet.explanation: Application service owns use-case logic; DbContext owns persistence. No extra interface layer. LINQ stays expressive and refactorable.

snippet.label: Domain-specific repository — when it earns its keep
snippet.explanation: Repository with domain-named methods hides complex query composition. Not generic CRUD — specific read model for one bounded context.

snippet.label: Anti-pattern — generic repository leaking IQueryable
snippet.explanation: Generic repository duplicating DbSet with IQueryable escape hatch provides no encapsulation. Microsoft EF docs recommend against this for new projects.

snippet.label: Integration testing without mocking repository
snippet.explanation: Test full stack with real EF provider (SQLite in-memory or Testcontainers PostgreSQL). Proves SQL translation and mapping — mock repository cannot.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: IRepository<T> for every entity — ceremony without value. Repository per DbSet but sharing one DbContext — just use DbContext. Mocking IRepository in unit tests while never testing LINQ — false confidence. Repository returning IQueryable to 'stay flexible' — couples callers to EF.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: measure whether repository layer reduces duplicate query bugs or just adds files. Code review: complex LINQ should live in one place — repository, specification, or private static query method. CQRS split: write side uses DbContext/aggregates; read side uses Dapper or raw SQL views with IOrderReadRepository — legitimate abstraction boundary. Open generic IRepository<> registration with Scrutor is acceptable only when team has strict rules against IQueryable leakage.

blocks.title: When to abstract
rows: Rare — EF provider swap is easier

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Insisting repository is always required for 'clean code.' Cannot explain DbContext is unit-of-work. Saying mock repository is sufficient testing for EF. Not knowing Microsoft's official stance: skip repository unless you need it.

interviewTakeaways: DbContext is already repository + unit of work — direct injection is Microsoft's recommended default for most APIs.
When to abstract: complex repeated queries, CQRS read models, domain-specific method names — not generic IRepository<T> CRUD.
Production tip: integration test with SQLite/Testcontainers; avoid mocking DbContext; encapsulate query logic in specifications.

60s: I inject DbContext into application services by default. Repository when query logic is complex or read model is separate. Generic IRepository is an anti-pattern — leaks IQueryable. Test with real EF provider, not mock repo.
Follow-up: how does CQRS change your data access layering?
commonPitfalls: Always use repository 'for testability' gets you rejected — mock repo does not test LINQ or SQL.

Strong answer: 'DbContext direct for most endpoints. Domain-named repository for complex reads or CQRS. Integration tests with Testcontainers. Abstraction earns its keep when it hides complexity, not CRUD.'
introducedIn: EF Core 1.0; community guidance evolved toward direct DbContext

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS @InjectRepository(Entity) is framework-mandated — closer to EF DbSet than custom IRepository. Custom repos in NestJS should still be domain-specific, not generic findAll.

Express has no standard — teams split routes/services/db modules manually. The EF debate maps to whether you wrap Prisma client in a repository class or call prisma.order.findMany directly in handlers.
